email.scenario: You arranged with the curator of the Ashfield City Archive to examine a set of nineteenth-century town maps for a history course project. You missed the appointment last Thursday because your train was cancelled, and the archive allows visitors into the reading room only by advance booking. All requests must be made in writing.
email.subject: Missed appointment on Thursday
bullets: Apologize for missing your appointment and explain what happened.
Propose a specific new date and time to view the maps.
Ask for clarification about what visitors may bring into the reading room.

academicDiscussion.professorPost: Most towns keep their public parks as closely mown lawns, but some have begun letting sections grow into rough meadow that is cut only once or twice a year. Supporters point to the wildflowers and insects that return; others argue that residents lose ground they actually use, and that an uncut park looks neglected. Councils in many towns are now being asked to decide. What do you think? Should towns let parts of their public parks grow wild instead of mowing them? Why or why not?

studentPosts.name: Hana
studentPosts.post: I would like to see it happen. The strip behind my old school was left uncut for two summers, and by the second year there were butterflies and moths I had never seen in town before. Cutting grass every week costs money and fuel, and almost nobody sits on that particular lawn anyway.

studentPosts.name: Julian
studentPosts.post: My neighborhood tried this, and the meadow simply became the part of the park that everyone avoided. The field where we played football on weekends disappeared, ticks turned up in the long grass, and older residents stopped walking there once the paths were overgrown. A park still has to be usable.
